failures.title: Mitsubishi 4B12 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Timing Chain Stretch - rattling on start‑up and rough idle
items.whatHappens: The 4B12 uses a timing chain that can stretch over time, particularly on engines with irregular oil changes. Symptoms include a persistent rattling noise on cold start, rough idle, and the triangle warning light. If the chain stretches beyond safe limits, it can jump a tooth, causing the engine to run roughly and potentially leading to valve damage - the 4B12 is an interference engine.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early (before the chain jumps), replacing the timing chain, tensioner, and guides is a standalone fix costing £700-£1,200. If the chain has jumped and valves have contacted pistons, the engine is typically unrebuildable - a replacement unit is required.

items.title: Ignition Coil Failure - misfires and loss of power
items.whatHappens: The 4B12's ignition coils (one per cylinder) can fail, particularly on higher‑mileage cars. Symptoms include engine misfire, rough idle, loss of power, and a flashing check engine light.
items.repairVsReplace: Ignition coils are individually replaceable - a straightforward fix costing £100-£200 per coil. Replacing all four as a set is recommended.

items.title: Oil Consumption - piston ring sticking (higher mileage)
items.whatHappens: Some 4B12 engines experience oil consumption due to piston rings sticking in the ring grooves, especially on cars with infrequent oil changes. Symptoms include blue smoke from the exhaust and needing to top up oil between services.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early, a decarbonisation treatment may help. If severe, piston ring replacement requires a full engine strip - often not cost‑effective compared to a replacement unit.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the 4B12
variants.intro: The 4B12 is Mitsubishi's 2.4‑litre MIVEC engine, part of the 4B1 family which includes the 4B10 (1.8L) and 4B11 (2.0L). It features MIVEC variable valve timing on both intake and exhaust camshafts, an aluminium block and head, and multi‑point fuel injection. Where to find the engine code: - On the engine block - a stamped plate on the front of the block - On the V5C registration document - under engine number - Via a Mitsubishi VIN decoder - the engine code is part of the vehicle identification Commonly confused codes: - 4B11 - the 2.0‑litre MIVEC engine (148 hp), found in lower‑spec Lancers and Outlanders; smaller displacement and lower output; not interchangeable without significant work - 4B10 - the 1.8‑litre MIVEC engine, found in some Asian‑market Lancers; not common in UK - 4B11T - the turbocharged 2.0‑litre engine from the Lancer Evolution X; completely different engine with different internals, turbo, and ECU; not interchangeable - 4G64 - the older 2.4‑litre SOHC engine that preceded the 4B12; different architecture and not a direct swap

relatives.description: the older 2.4‑litre SOHC engine that preceded the 4B12, found in earlier Mitsubishi models like the first‑gen Outlander, earlier Lancers, and Galants. The 4G64 had a cast‑iron block and SOHC cylinder head design; the 4B12 introduced the modern DOHC aluminium block architecture with MIVEC, offering better performance and fuel efficiency. [4G64 Engine - /mitsubishi/4g64-engine/]

the smaller displacement sibling of the 4B12, used in lower‑spec Lancers, Outlanders, and other Mitsubishi models. The 4B11 produces 148 hp and has a shorter stroke (86mm vs 97mm). If your Lancer or Outlander is a 2.0‑litre rather than 2.4, this is the page you need. [4B11 Engine - /mitsubishi/4b11-engine/]
the 1.8‑litre entry‑level MIVEC engine, used in some Asian‑market Lancers and other models. Not commonly found in UK spec cars. [4B10 Engine - /mitsubishi/4b10-engine/]

the turbocharged MIVEC engine from the Lancer Evolution X. The 4B11T shares the same block architecture but has forged internals, lower compression ratio, direct injection, and a massive turbocharger. It is a completely different engine; not interchangeable with the naturally aspirated 4B12. [4B11T Engine - /mitsubishi/4b11t-engine/]

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement 4B12 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: ** A used 4B12 makes sense for older Outlanders and Lancers where a reconditioned unit would exceed the vehicle's value. Used units are widely available from breakers and can cost around £1,490. However, they will almost certainly require a new timing chain kit and ignition coils - budget for those repairs. Only buy with documented service history and a compression test. Used engines

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: ** A proper 4B12 recon addresses the engine's known weaknesses: new timing chain, tensioner, guides, piston rings (if needed), and a full set of ignition coils. This is the right call for owners who want a reliable, long‑lasting unit - the 4B12 is fundamentally robust when properly refreshed. Expect £1,995-£2,500 with 12-24 months warranty. Reconditioned engines

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: ** A full 4B12 rebuild is rarely justified given the low cost of used and reconditioned units. It is only sensible for owners of rare variants or those who want to upgrade with forged internals. Costs exceed £2,500-£3,500. Rebuilt engines

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: ** Our vetted UK Mitsubishi specialists offer supply‑only or full supply‑and‑fit - 12‑month warranty on reconditioned units, nationwide delivery. Supply and fit
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: ** The 4B12 sits in Mitsubishi models now worth £2,000-£8,000 depending on age and mileage. A reconditioned 4B12 at £1,995-£2,500 represents 25-60% of vehicle value - a significant investment. For a high‑mileage Outlander worth under £3,000, a used unit with a new timing chain kit may be the most sensible option. Evaluate the car's overall condition before committing.

items.question: How much does a 4B12 engine replacement cost in the UK?
items.answer: A reconditioned 4B12 supply‑only costs £1,995-£2,500, with fitted prices from £2,445 to £2,950 depending on labour and parts. Used units cost £1,490-£1,800 but may require timing chain work. Rebuilt units may exceed £2,500-£3,500. Warranty is typically 12-24 months on reconditioned/rebuilt units.

items.question: What are the common problems with the 4B12 engine?
items.answer: The most documented failures are timing chain stretch (rattling on start‑up) and ignition coil failure (misfires, rough idle). Timing chain tensioner failure can destroy the engine if ignored - the 4B12 is an interference engine. Ignition coil failure is cheap to fix but causes drivability issues. Oil consumption can occur on higher‑mileage units with poor service history.

items.question: Which Mitsubishi models have the 4B12 engine?
items.answer: The 4B12 was fitted to the Mitsubishi Outlander (II and III), Lancer (VIII, including Sportback), ASX, and Delica D5 from 2006-2016. It was also used in the Citroën C‑Crosser and Peugeot 4007. It is the 2.4‑litre MIVEC petrol engine, distinct from the 2.0‑litre 4B11.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned 4B12?
items.answer: A reconditioned 4B12 is the safer choice because it addresses the engine's known weak points (timing chain, tensioner, piston rings, coils) and comes with a warranty. Used units are cheaper but will almost certainly require a new timing chain kit. For older Outlanders worth under £3,000, a used unit may be the only viable option.

items.question: How do I know if my Mitsubishi has the 4B12 or the 4B11?
items.answer: The engine code is stamped on the block (front of the block) and listed on your V5C or via a Mitsubishi VIN decoder. The 4B12 is 2.4‑litre and produces 168-172 hp. The 4B11 is 2.0‑litre and produces 148 hp. The 4B11T is the turbocharged Evolution X engine - completely different.
bullets: The 4B11T is the turbocharged Evolution X engine - completely different.

items.question: Is the 4B12 a reliable engine?
items.answer: The 4B12 is considered a robust engine when properly maintained, but timing chain and coil issues are common on higher‑mileage units. A well‑maintained 4B12 with regular oil changes (using 5W‑30 or 0W‑20) can exceed 150,000 miles. The timing chain tensioner is the main weakness - replacing it preventatively is recommended.
